dhpak2.7:2.1: “Through heedfulness did Maghavā attain leadership,” {1.263} this Dhamma teaching was given by the
dhpak2.7:2.2: Teacher while in residence at a Gabled Hall near Vesālī with reference to Sakka, the Lord of the Devas.
dhpak2.7:3.1: For a Licchavi named Mahāli, who lived at Vesālī, hearing the Teacher recite the Discourse entitled Sakka’s
dhpak2.7:3.2: Question, thought to himself: “The Sambuddha has described the great glory of Sakka. Has the Teacher seen Sakka?
dhpak2.7:3.3: Or has he not seen Sakka? Is the Teacher acquainted with Sakka? Or is he not acquainted with Sakka? I will ask
dhpak2.7:3.4: him.” So the Licchavi Mahāli drew near to where the Fortunate One was, and having drawn near, worshipped the
dhpak2.7:3.5: Fortunate One and sat down on one side. And having [28.314] sat down on one side, the Licchavi Mahāli spoke thus to
dhpak2.7:3.6: the Fortunate One: “Venerable Sir, has the Fortunate One seen Sakka, the Lord of the Devas?” {1.264} – “Yes, Mahāli,
dhpak2.7:3.7: I have indeed seen Sakka, the Lord of the Devas.” – “Venerable Sir, it must certainly have been a counterfeit of
dhpak2.7:3.8: Sakka; for, venerable Sir, it is a difficult matter to see Sakka, the Lord of the Devas.” – “Nevertheless, Mahāli, I know
dhpak2.7:3.9: Sakka; I know what qualities made him Sakka; I know by the cultivation of what qualities Sakka attained Sakkaship.
dhpak2.7:4.1: Mahāli, in a previous state of existence Sakka, the Lord of the Devas,
dhpak2.7:4.2: was a human being, a youth named Magha; therefore is he called Maghavā.
dhpak2.7:4.3: Mahāli, in a previous state of existence Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, was a
dhpak2.7:4.4: human being who gave gifts (pure dānaṁ adāsi); therefore is he called Purindada.
dhpak2.7:4.5: Mahāli, in a previous state of existence Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, was a
dhpak2.7:4.6: human being, who gave alms respectfully (sakkaccaṁ); therefore is he called Sakka.
dhpak2.7:4.7: Mahāli, in a previous state of existence Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, was a
dhpak2.7:4.8: human being who gave a dwelling-place (āvasathaṁ); therefore is he called Vāsava.
dhpak2.7:4.9: Mahāli, in a previous state of existence Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, was a human being who could
dhpak2.7:4.10: think of as many as a thousand things (sahassaṁ atthaṁ) in an instant; therefore is he called Sahassakkha.
dhpak2.7:4.11: Mahāli, Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, has an Asura maiden named Sujā to wife; therefore is he called Sujampati.
dhpak2.7:4.12: Mahāli, Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, bears sway as lord and master
dhpak2.7:4.13: over the Devas of the Thirty-Three; therefore is he called King of Devas.
dhpak2.7:5.1: Mahāli, Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, in a previous state of existence as a human being took upon himself
dhpak2.7:5.2: and fulfilled seven vows. Because he took upon himself and fulfilled these seven vows, Sakka {1.265}
dhpak2.7:5.3: attained Sakkaship. Now what were the seven? ‘So long as I live, may I be the support of my mother and
dhpak2.7:5.4: father. So long as I live, may I honor my elders. So long as I live, may I speak gentle words. So long as I
dhpak2.7:5.5: live, may I never give way to backbiting. So long as I live, may I live the life of a householder with heart
dhpak2.7:5.6: free from taint of avarice, generous in renunciation of what is mine, with open hand, delighting in
dhpak2.7:5.7: liberality, attentive to petitions, delighting in the distribution of alms. So long as I live, may I speak the
dhpak2.7:5.8: truth. So long as I live, may I be free from anger. Should anger spring up within me, may I quickly suppress
dhpak2.7:5.9: it.’ Mahāli, Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, in a previous state of existence took upon himself and fulfilled
dhpak2.7:5.10: seven vows. Because he took upon himself and fulfilled these seven vows, Sakka attained Sakkaship. [28.315]
dhpak2.7:6.1: A man who supports mother and father, who pays respect to elders in the clan, who is gentle and kind
dhpak2.7:6.2: in conversing, who has abandoned speech that’s divisive, devoted to removing selfishness, who is
dhpak2.7:6.3: truthful, overcoming anger, that one even the Devas of Tāvatiṁsa speak, saying that he is a good person.”
dhpak2.7:7.1: When the Teacher said: “This, Mahāli, was what Sakka did in his previous existence as the youth Magha.”
dhpak2.7:7.2: Mahāli, desiring to hear the whole story of his conduct, asked the Teacher: “Venerable Sir, how did the
dhpak2.7:7.3: youth Magha conduct himself?” – “Well then,” said the Teacher, “listen.” So saying, he related the following
dhpak2.7:8.1: In times long past a youth named Magha lived in the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha. {1.266}
dhpak2.7:8.2: One day he went to the place where the business of the village was carried on, removed with his foot the
dhpak2.7:8.3: dust from the place where he stood, and having made a comfortable place for himself, stood there. Thereupon
dhpak2.7:8.4: another struck him with his arm, pushed him aside, and took his place. But instead of becoming angry at the
dhpak2.7:8.5: man, he made another comfortable place for himself and stood there. Thereupon another struck him with his
dhpak2.7:8.6: arm, pushed him away, and took his place. But neither did he allow himself to become angry at this man; he
dhpak2.7:8.7: merely made another comfortable place for himself and stood there. In like manner one man after another came out
dhpak2.7:8.8: of his house, struck him with his arm, and pushed him away from the place which he had cleared for himself.
dhpak2.7:9.1: The youth thought to himself: “All these men appear to be pleased. Since this work of mine conduces to
dhpak2.7:9.2: the happiness of men, it must be a meritorious work.” So on the following day he took a spade and
dhpak2.7:9.3: cleared a space as big as a threshing-floor, whereupon all the men came and stood there. In cold weather
dhpak2.7:9.4: he built a fire to warm them, and in hot weather he gave them water. Then he thought to himself: “A
dhpak2.7:9.5: pleasant place is dear to all, and to none is it displeasing. From now on it is necessary for me to go about
dhpak2.7:9.6: making the road smooth and even.” So early in the morning he started out to make the road smooth and even,
dhpak2.7:9.7: cutting down and removing all the branches of trees that needed to be removed. Thus did he spend his time.
dhpak2.7:10.1: Another man saw him and said to him: “Master, what are you doing?” He replied: “Master, I am treading the
dhpak2.7:10.2: path that leads to heaven (sagga).” – “I also am your companion.” – “Be my companion, master; heaven is a
dhpak2.7:10.3: pleasant place for many.” {1.267} Seeing these two, a third man asked the same question, received the
dhpak2.7:10.4: same answer, and joined them; then a fourth, then a fifth, until finally there were thirty-three. [28.316]
dhpak2.7:11.1: All these men worked together with spades and other tools and made the road smooth and even for a distance of one
dhpak2.7:11.2: or two leagues. The village headman saw them and thought to himself: “These men are all following the wrong
dhpak2.7:11.3: occupation. If they would only fetch fish and flesh from the forest, or indulge in strong drink, or do something
dhpak2.7:11.4: else of the sort, I should make something by it.” So he sent for them and asked them: “What is it you are doing?” –
dhpak2.7:11.5: “Treading the path to heaven, master.” – “That is no proper occupation for men living the lives of laymen. What you
dhpak2.7:11.6: should do is to bring fish and flesh from the forest, indulge in strong drink, and have a general good time.” But they
dhpak2.7:11.7: refused to follow his suggestion, and the more he urged them, the more firmly they refused to do as he suggested.
dhpak2.7:12.1: Finally the village headman became angry. “I will destroy them,” he said. So he went to the king and said to
dhpak2.7:12.2: him: “Your majesty, I see a band of thieves going about.” The king replied: “Go catch them and bring them before
dhpak2.7:12.3: me.” So the village headman arrested the thirty-three youths and hauled them before the king. Without instituting
dhpak2.7:12.4: an inquiry into their conduct, the king gave the following order: “Have them trampled to death by an elephant.”
dhpak2.7:13.1: Thereupon Magha admonished his companions as follows: “Friends, we have no refuge but
dhpak2.7:13.2: loving-kindness. Therefore let your hearts be tranquil. Cherish anger towards no one. Let your
dhpak2.7:13.3: hearts be full of loving-kindness for the king and the village headman and the elephant that
dhpak2.7:13.4: tramples you under his feet, and for yourselves.” The thirty-three youths followed the admonition of
dhpak2.7:13.5: their leader. Such was the power of their loving-kindness that the elephant dared not approach them.
dhpak2.7:14.1: When the king heard of this, he said: {1.268} “If the elephant sees so many men, he will not venture to trample
dhpak2.7:14.2: them under his feet. Have the men covered with heavy matting, and then order the elephant to trample them.” So
dhpak2.7:14.3: the village headman had the men covered with heavy matting and drove the elephant forwards to trample them. But
dhpak2.7:14.4: when the elephant was yet a long way off, he turned round and went back. When the king heard what had happened,
dhpak2.7:14.5: he thought to himself: “There must be some reason for this.” So he caused the thirty-three youths to be brought
dhpak2.7:14.6: before him and asked them: “Friends, is there anything which you have failed to receive at my hands?” – “Your
dhpak2.7:14.7: majesty, what do you mean?” – “I am informed that you are a band of thieves and that you rove about the forest
dhpak2.7:14.8: committing depredations.” – “Your majesty, who said that?” – “Friends, the village headman so informed me.” [28.317]
dhpak2.7:15.1: “Your majesty, it is not true that we are thieves. The fact is, we are clearing a path to heaven for
dhpak2.7:15.2: ourselves, and we do this and that. The village headman tried to persuade us to adopt a wicked mode of life,
dhpak2.7:15.3: and when we refused to follow his suggestions, he became angry at us and determined to destroy us. That is
dhpak2.7:15.4: why he said this about us.” – “Friends, this animal knows your good qualities; but I, who am a man, was
dhpak2.7:15.5: unable to discern them. Pardon me.” So saying, the delighted king made the village headman their slave,
dhpak2.7:15.6: together with his children and wife, gave them a riding-elephant, and presented that village to them to do with
dhpak2.7:15.7: as they saw fit. The thirty-three youths thought: “Even in this life the advantage to be derived from the
dhpak2.7:15.8: performance of works of merit is clearly to be seen.” And mounting the elephant by turns, they rode about the village.
dhpak2.7:16.1: As they went about the village, they took counsel together, {1.269} saying: “It is our duty to
dhpak2.7:16.2: perform yet more abundant works of merit. What shall we do?” Thereupon the following thought occurred
dhpak2.7:16.3: to them: “Let us build at the crossing of the four highways a rest-house for the multitude, making it
dhpak2.7:16.4: secure and strong.” So they summoned a builder and ordered him to build a hall for them. And because
dhpak2.7:16.5: desire for women had departed from them, they resolved to give women no share in the building of the hall.
dhpak2.7:17.1: Now there were four women living in Magha’s house, Nandā, Cittā, Sudhammā, and Sujā. Sudhammā went
dhpak2.7:17.2: secretly to the builder, gave him a bribe, and said to him: “Friend, give me the principal share in the
dhpak2.7:17.3: building of this hall.” – “Very well,” replied the builder, agreeing to her proposal. Accordingly he
dhpak2.7:17.4: first marked a tree out of which to make a pinnacle, felled it, and laid it aside to season. Then he hewed
dhpak2.7:17.5: it and planed it and bored it, and having fashioned it in the form of a pinnacle, carved the following
dhpak2.7:17.6: inscription on it: “This is the Hall of Sudhammā.” Having so done, he wrapped it in a cloth and laid it aside.
dhpak2.7:18.1: Now when he had completed the hall and the day came to erect the pinnacle, he said to the thirty-three
dhpak2.7:18.2: youths: “Noble sirs, there is something we have forgotten.” – “What is it, sir?” – “A pinnacle.” – “Let us
dhpak2.7:18.3: procure one.” – “It is impossible to make one out of a freshly hewn tree. We should procure for a pinnacle a
dhpak2.7:18.4: tree felled long ago and laid away to season.” – “What had we best do under the circumstances?” – “If in
dhpak2.7:18.5: anybody’s house there is a completed pinnacle which has been laid away to season and which is for sale, {1.270} that
dhpak2.7:18.6: is the thing for you to search for.” So they searched everywhere, and finding [28.318] what they wanted in the house
dhpak2.7:18.7: of Sudhammā, offered her a thousand coins for it. But they were unable to secure it for the price they offered.
dhpak2.7:19.1: Sudhammā said: “If you will give me a share in the building of the hall, I will give you the pinnacle.”
dhpak2.7:19.2: But they replied: “We have resolved to give women no share in the building of this hall.” Thereupon the
dhpak2.7:19.3: builder said to them: “Noble sirs, what are you doing? With the exception of the world of Brahma, there is
dhpak2.7:19.4: no place from which women are excluded. Take the pinnacle, for if you do, our work will speedily be
dhpak2.7:19.5: finished.” – “Very well,” said they. So they took the pinnacle and completed the hall. And they divided the
dhpak2.7:19.6: hall into three parts, reserving one chamber for the powerful, another for the poor, and another for the sick.
dhpak2.7:20.1: Then the thirty-three youths built thirty-three seats, and
dhpak2.7:20.2: having so done, gave the following orders to the elephant:
dhpak2.7:20.3: “If a visitor comes and sits down in a seat, take him and
dhpak2.7:20.4: lodge him in the house of whoever built and owns that seat.
dhpak2.7:20.5: It then becomes the duty of the owner of that seat to see that his guest’s feet and back are rubbed, to provide
dhpak2.7:20.6: him with food both hard and soft, and with lodging; to perform for him, in fact, all the duties of hospitality.”
dhpak2.7:20.7: Accordingly, whenever a visitor came, the elephant would take him and
dhpak2.7:20.8: conduct him to the house of the owner of the seat in which he had sat,
dhpak2.7:20.9: and the owner of the seat would on that day perform for him all the duties of hospitality.
dhpak2.7:21.1: Magha planted a koviḷāra tree near the hall and built a stone seat at the foot of the
dhpak2.7:21.2: koviḷāra tree. All those who entered the hall looked at the pinnacle, read the inscription,
dhpak2.7:21.3: and said: “This is the Hall of Sudhammā.” The names of the thirty-three youths did not appear.
dhpak2.7:22.1: Nandā thought to herself: “The youths who built this hall resolved to deprive us of a share in the building
dhpak2.7:22.2: thereof. {1.271} But Sudhammā by her own cleverness obtained a share. I also ought to do something. What can I do?”
dhpak2.7:22.3: Thereupon the following thought occurred to her: “Those who come to the hall should be provided with water for
dhpak2.7:22.4: drinking and water for bathing. I will have a place dug for a pool.” Accordingly Nandā caused a bathing-pool to be built.
dhpak2.7:23.1: Cittā thought to herself: “Sudhammā has given a pinnacle, and Nandā has caused a swimming-pool to be
dhpak2.7:23.2: built. What can I do?” Thereupon the following thought occurred to her: “After those who come to the
dhpak2.7:23.3: hall have drunk water and bathed, they should be decked with garlands when they are ready to depart.
dhpak2.7:23.4: I will cause a flower garden to be laid out.” So Cittā caused a beautiful flower garden to be laid
dhpak2.7:23.5: out. So many and so various were the flowers that grew therein [28.319] that it was impossible for
dhpak2.7:23.6: anyone to say: “Such and such a flower-bearing or fruit-bearing tree does not grow in this garden.”
dhpak2.7:24.1: Now Sujā thought to herself: “I am the daughter of the brother of the mother of Magha and likewise
dhpak2.7:24.2: the wife of Magha. The merit of the work he has wrought accrues to me only, and the merit of the work
dhpak2.7:24.3: I have wrought accrues to him only.” Accordingly she did nothing but spend her time adorning herself.
dhpak2.7:25.1: Thus did Magha minister to his mother and father, honor his elders in the
dhpak2.7:25.2: household, speak the truth, avoid harsh words, avoid backbiting, put away
dhpak2.7:25.3: avarice, suppress anger. Even thus did he fulfill the seven vows, as it is said: {1.272}
dhpak2.7:26.1: A man who supports mother and father, who pays respect to elders in the clan, who is gentle and kind
dhpak2.7:26.2: in conversing, who has abandoned speech that’s divisive, devoted to removing selfishness, who is
dhpak2.7:26.3: truthful, overcoming anger, that one even the Devas of Tāvatiṁsa speak, saying that he is a good person.
dhpak2.7:27.1: Having attained so praiseworthy a state, Magha, upon reaching the end of the term of life
dhpak2.7:27.2: allotted to him, was reborn in the Realm of the Thirty-Three as Sakka, the Lord of the
dhpak2.7:27.3: Devas. His companions were likewise reborn there. The builder was reborn as Devaputta Vissakamma.
dhpak2.7:28.1: Now at that time there were Asuras dwelling in the Realm of the Thirty-Three, and when they learned
dhpak2.7:28.2: that new gods had been reborn there, they prepared celestial drink. But Sakka gave orders to his
dhpak2.7:28.3: retinue that no one should drink thereof. The Asuras, however, drank freely and became intoxicated.
dhpak2.7:28.4: Thereupon Sakka thought to himself: “Why should I share my kingdom with these Asuras?” Forthwith, giving
dhpak2.7:28.5: a sign to his retinue, he caused them to pick up the Asuras by the heels and fling them into the Great
dhpak2.7:28.6: Ocean. So the Asuras fell headlong into the Ocean. By the power of their merit there sprang up at the foot
dhpak2.7:28.7: of Mount Sineru a palace called the Asura palace and the tree that is called the Pied Trumpet-flower.
dhpak2.7:29.1: When the conflict between the gods and the Asuras was over and the Asuras
dhpak2.7:29.2: had been defeated, there came into existence the city of the Thirty-Three.
dhpak2.7:29.3: The distance from the eastern gate to the western gate was ten thousand
dhpak2.7:29.4: leagues, and the distance from the southern gate to the northern gate was the same.
dhpak2.7:29.5: Now this city was provided with a thousand gates and was adorned with gardens and pools,
dhpak2.7:29.6: and in the midst thereof, {1.273} as the fruit of the building of the hall, there arose a palace called the
dhpak2.7:29.7: Palace of Victory. Its height was seven hundred leagues, and it was decked with banners three hundred leagues long.
dhpak2.7:29.8: On staffs of gold were banners of jewels, and on staffs of jewels were [28.320] banners of gold; on staffs
dhpak2.7:29.9: of coral were banners of pearls, and on staffs of pearls were banners of coral; on staffs of the seven
dhpak2.7:29.10: precious stones were banners of the seven precious stones. A banner three hundred leagues high stood in the center.
dhpak2.7:29.11: Such was the palace that arose as the fruit of the building of the hall; a
dhpak2.7:29.12: thousand leagues was its height, and it was composed of the seven precious stones.
dhpak2.7:30.1: As the result of the planting of the koviḷāra tree, there arose the coral tree, three hundred leagues in
dhpak2.7:30.2: circumference. As the result of the building of the stone seat, there came into existence at the foot of
dhpak2.7:30.3: the coral tree the Paṇḍukambala stone throne, reddish like a jayasumana flower, sixty leagues in length,
dhpak2.7:30.4: fifty leagues in breadth, and fifteen leagues thick. When Sakka sits down on this throne, half his body
dhpak2.7:30.5: sinks into the throne; when he rises, it is all above ground. The elephant was reborn as god Erāvaṇa.
dhpak2.7:30.6: There are no animals in the Deva Realm; so when he went into the garden to play, he would quit his form as
dhpak2.7:30.7: a god and become the elephant Erāvaṇa, a hundred and fifty leagues in size. For the thirty-three youths,
dhpak2.7:30.8: Erāvaṇa created thirty-three waterpots, each measuring from half to three quarters of a league around.
dhpak2.7:31.1: In the center of all, Erāvaṇa created for Sakka a waterpot
dhpak2.7:31.2: called Sudassana. It was thirty leagues in circumference,
dhpak2.7:31.3: and above it was a canopy, twelve leagues in size, made entirely of precious stones.
dhpak2.7:31.4: {1.274} At regular intervals about the canopy there arose
dhpak2.7:31.5: banners a league in length, made entirely of the seven precious stones.
dhpak2.7:31.6: And from the lower edge of each banner depended a row of tinkling bells,
dhpak2.7:31.7: which, when they were shaken by the gentle wind, gave forth sweet music like the mingled
dhpak2.7:31.8: strains of the music of the five kinds of instruments or the singing of the celestial choir.
dhpak2.7:31.9: In the center of the pavilion was prepared for Sakka a jeweled couch a league in length. There Sakka sat.
dhpak2.7:31.10: The thirty-three gods sat on jeweled couches in their own waterpots.
dhpak2.7:31.11: Each vessel bore seven tusks, each fifty leagues long;
dhpak2.7:31.12: each tusk bore seven lotus-tanks; each lotus-tank bore
dhpak2.7:31.13: seven lotus-plants; each lotus-plant bore seven flowers; each
dhpak2.7:31.14: flower, seven leaves; and on each leaf danced seven Accharās.
dhpak2.7:31.15: Thus on all sides round about for a space of fifty leagues there were dancing-assemblies poised on
dhpak2.7:31.16: elephants’ tusks. Such was the glory in the enjoyment of which lived Sakka, the Lord of the Devas.
dhpak2.7:32.1: When Sudhammā died, she was also reborn there. And at the same time there came into existence Sudhammā, the
dhpak2.7:32.2: meeting hall of the Devas, nine hundred leagues in extent, than which exists no other place more charming.
dhpak2.7:32.3: {1.275} Here, on eight days of the month, is taught [28.321] the Dhamma. Unto this day, when men behold a
dhpak2.7:32.4: charming place, they say: “It is like Sudhammā, the meeting hall of the Devas.” When Nandā died, she also was
dhpak2.7:32.5: reborn there. And at the same time there came into existence a lotus-tank called Nandā, five hundred leagues in
dhpak2.7:32.6: extent. When Cittā died, she also was reborn there. And at the same time there came into existence Cittā’s
dhpak2.7:32.7: creeper-grove, five hundred leagues in extent. There they conduct the gods in whom the signs of impending death have
dhpak2.7:32.8: appeared, and walk about charming them. But when Sujā died, she was reborn as a crane in a certain mountain-cave.
dhpak2.7:33.1: Sakka surveyed his wives and considered within himself: “Sudhammā has been reborn here and likewise
dhpak2.7:33.2: Nandā and Cittā. Now where has Sujā been reborn?” Perceiving that she had been reborn as a crane in
dhpak2.7:33.3: a mountain-cave, he thought to himself: “Because she wrought no work of merit, the foolish girl has
dhpak2.7:33.4: been reborn as a bird. It is my duty to have her perform some work of merit and bring her here.”
dhpak2.7:34.1: So saying, he laid aside his proper form, and assuming a disguise, he went to her and asked: “What are
dhpak2.7:34.2: you doing here?” – “But, master, who are you?” – “I am your husband, Magha.” – “Where were you reborn,
dhpak2.7:34.3: husband?” – “I was reborn in the Realm of the Thirty-Three. Do you know where your companions were
dhpak2.7:34.4: reborn?” – “No, husband, I do not.” – “They also were reborn near me in the Realm of the Thirty-Three.
dhpak2.7:34.5: Should you like to see your companions?” – “How can I get there?” Said Sakka: “I will carry you there.”
dhpak2.7:35.1: Placing her in the palm of his hand, he carried her to the Deva Realm and set her free on the bank
dhpak2.7:35.2: of the lotus-tank named Nandā. Then he said to the other three: “Should you like to see your
dhpak2.7:35.3: companion Sujā?” – “Sire, where is she?” {1.276} – “On the bank of the lotus-tank named Nandā.” So the
dhpak2.7:35.4: three went and looked at her. “Alas!” they cried out, “see what has been the result of the noble woman’s
dhpak2.7:35.5: spending her life in the adornment of self! Look now at her beak! Look at her feet! Look at her legs!
dhpak2.7:35.6: She presents a beautiful appearance indeed!” Thus did they ridicule her. Having so done, they departed.
dhpak2.7:36.1: Sakka went once more to her and said: “Did you see your companions?” – “Yes,” replied Sujā: “I saw them.
dhpak2.7:36.2: They ridiculed me and then went their way. Take me back again.” So Sakka took her back again, set her free
dhpak2.7:36.3: in the water, and then asked her: “Did you see their celestial glory?” – “Yes, Sire, I did.” – “You also
dhpak2.7:36.4: should employ such means as will enable you to obtain rebirth there.” – “Sire, what shall I do?” – “If I
dhpak2.7:36.5: admonish you, will you keep my admonition?” [28.322] – “Yes, Sire, I will keep your admonition.” So Sakka
dhpak2.7:36.6: taught her the five precepts. Having so done, he said to her: “Be zealous in keeping the precepts,” and departed.
dhpak2.7:37.1: Thenceforth she sought after and ate only such fish as had died a natural death. After a few days had passed,
dhpak2.7:37.2: Sakka determined to test her. So he went, and taking the form of a fish, lay down on the surface of the sand,
dhpak2.7:37.3: pretending to be dead. When she saw the fish, thinking that it was dead, she took it in her beak. Just as she
dhpak2.7:37.4: was about to swallow the fish, it wriggled its tail. The instant she discovered the fish was alive she
dhpak2.7:37.5: released it in the water. Sakka waited a little while, and then lay down before her on his back once more. Again
dhpak2.7:37.6: thinking it was a dead fish, she took it in her beak. But just as she was about to swallow the fish, it moved the
dhpak2.7:37.7: tip of its tail. The instant she saw the fish move its tail she knew it was alive, and therefore let it go.
dhpak2.7:38.1: When Sakka had thus tested her three times and had satisfied himself that she was keeping the
dhpak2.7:38.2: precepts faithfully, he revealed his identity to her and said: “I came here for the purpose of
dhpak2.7:38.3: testing you. You are keeping the precepts faithfully. If you continue thus faithfully to keep them,
dhpak2.7:38.4: {1.277} you will before long be reborn near me. Be heedful.” So saying these words, he departed.
dhpak2.7:39.1: Thenceforth she used for food either fish that had died a natural death or none at all. After
dhpak2.7:39.2: only a few days had passed, she shriveled up and died, and as the fruit of her virtuous conduct
dhpak2.7:39.3: was reborn at Bārāṇasī as the daughter of a potter. When she was about fifteen or sixteen years
dhpak2.7:39.4: old, Sakka considered within himself: “Where has she been reborn?” Perceiving that she had been
dhpak2.7:39.5: reborn at Bārāṇasī as the daughter of a potter, he said to himself: “I ought now to go to her.”
dhpak2.7:40.1: So filling a cart with the seven kinds of precious stones disguised as cucumbers, he drove into the city of
dhpak2.7:40.2: Bārāṇasī. “Come, get cucumbers!” he cried, as he entered the street. But when people came to him with pulses
dhpak2.7:40.3: and the like in their hands, he said: “I do not part with my cucumbers for a price.” – “On what terms do you
dhpak2.7:40.4: part with them, then?” the people asked him. “I give them to the woman that keeps the precepts,” he replied.
dhpak2.7:40.5: “Master, what do you mean by ‘precepts’? Are they black or blue or of some other color?” – “You don’t even know
dhpak2.7:40.6: what precepts are; much less will you keep them. I will give my cucumbers to the woman who keeps the precepts.”
dhpak2.7:41.1: “Master, there is a potter’s daughter who is always going about saying: ‘I keep the precepts.’ Give
dhpak2.7:41.2: them to her.” The potter’s [28.323] daughter said to him: “Very well, master, give them to me.” – “Who
dhpak2.7:41.3: are you?” – “I have never failed to keep the five precepts.” {1.278} – “For you alone have I brought
dhpak2.7:41.4: these,” said Sakka. And driving his cart to her house, he presented to her, in the guise of cucumbers,
dhpak2.7:41.5: celestial treasure which cannot be taken away by others. And making his identity known to her, he said:
dhpak2.7:41.6: “Here is wealth sufficient for you to live on. Keep the five precepts unbroken.” So saying, he departed.
dhpak2.7:42.1: At the end of her existence as a potter’s daughter she was reborn in the world of the Asuras as the
dhpak2.7:42.2: daughter of Vepacitti, king of Asuras, a bitter enemy of Sakka. Since she had kept the precepts in
dhpak2.7:42.3: two successive existences, she was fair of form, her skin was of a golden hue, and she was endowed
dhpak2.7:42.4: with beauty and comeliness the like of which had never been seen. Vepacitti, king of Asuras, said to
dhpak2.7:42.5: all the Asura princes who sought her in marriage: “You are not fit to marry my daughter.” Having thus
dhpak2.7:42.6: refused to give her in marriage to any of the Asura princes, he said: “My daughter shall choose for
dhpak2.7:42.7: herself such a husband as she sees fit.” So saying, he assembled the host of Asuras, and placing a garland
dhpak2.7:42.8: of flowers in the hand of his daughter, said to her: “Choose for yourself a husband who suits you.”
dhpak2.7:43.1: At that moment Sakka looked to see where she had been reborn. Perceiving what was taking place, he assumed the
dhpak2.7:43.2: form of an aged Asura and went and stood in the outer circle of the assembled company. The daughter of
dhpak2.7:43.3: Vepacitti looked this way and that. Suddenly, because in a previous state of existence she had lived with
dhpak2.7:43.4: Sakka, she was overwhelmed as by a mighty torrent by the power of the love for him which sprang up within her.
dhpak2.7:43.5: And crying out: “He is my husband!” she threw the garland of flowers over his head. Said the Asuras: “For a long
dhpak2.7:43.6: time our king has been unable to find a husband suitable for his daughter. Now, however, he has found one. This
dhpak2.7:43.7: fellow is old enough to be his daughter’s grandfather.” {1.279} And they departed, hanging their heads with shame.
dhpak2.7:44.1: Sakka took her by the hand, cried out: “I am Sakka,” and flew up into the air. The Asuras exclaimed: “We
dhpak2.7:44.2: have been fooled by Old Sakka,” and started up in pursuit. Mātali the charioteer brought up the chariot
dhpak2.7:44.3: called the Chariot of Victory and stopped by the way. Thereupon Sakka assisted his bride to mount and set
dhpak2.7:44.4: out for the city of the Devas. Now when they reached the forest of the Silk-cotton Trees, the Garuḍa
dhpak2.7:44.5: fledglings, hearing the sound of the chariot and fearing they would be crushed to death, cried out. [28.324]
dhpak2.7:45.1: When Sakka heard their cries, he asked Mātali: “What are they that are crying?” – “Garuḍa fledglings, Sire,” –
dhpak2.7:45.2: “Why are they crying?” – “They hear the sound of the chariot and fear they will be crushed to death.” – “Let not
dhpak2.7:45.3: so numerous a host perish, crushed by the impact of the chariot, because of me alone. Cause the chariot to turn
dhpak2.7:45.4: back.” Thereupon Mātali gave the sign with the lash to the thousand Sindh horses and caused the chariot to turn back.
dhpak2.7:46.1: When the Asuras saw that the chariot had turned back, they said: “Old Sakka started out in
dhpak2.7:46.2: flight from the city of the Asuras, but has just caused his chariot to turn back. Doubtless he
dhpak2.7:46.3: has received reinforcements.” And turning back, the Asuras entered the city of the Asuras by the
dhpak2.7:46.4: same road by which they had come out and nevermore lifted up their heads. Sakka bore the Asura
dhpak2.7:46.5: maiden Sujā to the city of the Devas and installed her as the chief of twenty-five million Accharās.
dhpak2.7:47.1: One day Sujā asked Sakka for a boon, saying: “Great king, in this Deva Realm I have neither
dhpak2.7:47.2: mother nor father nor brother nor sister; therefore pray take me with you wherever you go.”
dhpak2.7:47.3: {1.280} – “Very well,” replied Sakka, promising to do for her as she had asked.
dhpak2.7:47.4: Thenceforth, when the tree that is called Pied Trumpet-flower blooms, the Asuras cry out: “Now is
dhpak2.7:47.5: the time when our heavenly coral tree blooms,” and straightaway they sally forth to attack Sakka.
dhpak2.7:47.6: Therefore Sakka provides protection to the Nāgas in the sea below, then
dhpak2.7:47.7: to the Supaṇṇas, the Kumbhaṇḍas, the Yakkhas, and the Four Great Kings.
dhpak2.7:47.8: And over all, for the purpose of averting disaster, he places before the gates
dhpak2.7:47.9: of the city of the Devas images of Indra bearing the thunderbolt in his hands.
dhpak2.7:47.10: When the Asuras, after defeating the Nāgas and the other supernatural beings approach the city
dhpak2.7:47.11: of the Devas and see the images of Indra, they cry out: “Sakka has made a sally,” and flee away.
dhpak2.7:48.1: Thus, Mahāli, the youth Magha adopted the way of heedfulness. Because he was so heedful, he obtained such
dhpak2.7:48.2: sovereignty so exalted and came to rule over the two worlds of the Devas. Heedfulness is praised by the
dhpak2.7:48.3: Buddhas and by others likewise. For it is through heedfulness that all attain the higher attainments, both
dhpak2.7:48.4: those that are of this world and those that transcend this world.” So saying, he pronounced the following verse:
dhpak2.7:49.1: Through heedfulness did Maghavā attain leadership of the gods, the
dhpak2.7:49.2: good always praise heedfulness, but heedlessness is always blamed.
dhpak2.7:51.1: At the conclusion of the verse the Licchavī Mahāli was established in the
dhpak2.7:51.2: fruition of Stream-entry, and many of the assembly became Stream-enterers and so on.
